title: Comparing Three Anomaly Detectors for False Data Injection in Real Aquaculture: PH, DO and Temperature Using Two Different Computer Vision Techniques
content: World population is growing and expected to increase to 9․7 billion by 2050․ Demand for prod-ucts‚ including food‚ may rise with world population growth․ Other factors affecting demand include climate change and growing consumer interest in protein-rich foods․ Fish are an im-portant source of nutrition for people around the world․ Supply issues for wild-caught fish exist․ Options to reduce fishing pressure on wild fish populations include expanding aquaculture pro-duction and other actions to decrease the demand for wild-caught fish․ Wireless and IoT tech-nologies are applied in aquaculture to boost production․ Advantages of wireless technologies for aquaculture operators include savings on labor costs from reduced water sample collection for other testing at fish farms․ Other key tests for fish farmers to consider include dissolved oxygen‚ pH‚ and water temperature tests․ These factors can affect the health and survival of fish․ Fish with low dissolved oxygen levels might be seen at the surface where more oxygen is available․ Improper pH and water temperatures can lead to other health issues for fish over time․ However‚ connected monitoring systems face other challenges for farmers․ Operations and maintenance decisions related to aeration and other water treatment systems are based in part on sensor data․ Sensor failures and cyberattacks can interfere with sensor data and lead connected monitoring systems to signal that water conditions are suitable for fish‚ even when fish are under stress․ Lack of accurate sensor data can delay farmers' recognition of fish stress until they observe physical signs of stress in fish․ Accurate sensor data is important to farmers' success․ Other tools farmers need include ways to detect possibly inaccurate sensor data and determine whether inaccurate sensor data results from sensor failures‚ genuine environmental changes‚ or cyberattacks․ The problem addressed in this paper is further complicated by cyberattacks on sensor output data used to monitor water quality․ This paper explores applications of two computer vision tech-niques‚ YOLOv8 and Grounding DINO‚ for fish monitoring․ Applications of YOLOv8 and Grounding DINO include counting and identifying fish at the water's surface․ Data from both computer vision techniques will be combined with dissolved oxygen data to evaluate the use of computer vision data to identify cyberattack-related anomalies in sensor outputs․ The compari-son considers detection metrics and other differences‚ including water quality factors such as DO and pH levels and temperature․ Researchers investigated the detection performance of three methods (Isolation Forest‚ One-Class SVM‚ and LOF) and the benefits of adding fish-surfacing information to these methods to detect false data injection attacks․ Other research questions in-clude physical challenges to detection‚ such as obscured camera views and other factors that could affect an attack detection system‚ including equipment malfunctions and natural water quality changes‚ to understand more about detecting cyberattacks in commercial fish farms․ An experiment to test research questions was conducted using 29 days of data collected for dissolved oxygen‚ pH‚ temperature‚ and fish surfacing observations from cameras․ Data from the first 14 days (20‚160 one-minute time periods) were used to develop models using Isolation Forest‚ One-Class SVM‚ and Local Outlier Factor techniques․ Data from three  days (4‚320 one-minute time periods) were used to establish threshold levels․ 23 different attack scenarios were conduct-ed over 13‚800 one-minute time periods starting with the attack․ Maximum F1 scores for all three water quality sensor variables for a given attack type were 0․184 for dissolved oxygen using LOF‚ 0․262 for pH using Isolation Forest‚ and 0․199 for temperature using LOF․ Adding fish population data using YOLO and Grounding DINO proxies improved F1 scores for dissolved oxygen using Isolation Forest from 0․072 to 0․414 and 0․468․
